Moon Capital Management an investment management company, recently released its Q3 2026 investor letter. A copy of the letter can be downloaded here. The letter reported that its equity portfolio gained approximately 4% during the first nine months of 2026, compared with an approximately 12% year-to-date return for the S&P 500. The firm noted that market gains remained narrow, with nearly half of S&P 500 constituents declining during the period and the median stock gaining only about 4%. Much of the letter focused on AI investment, as major technology companies are expected to spend approximately $1.2 trillion on capital expenditures in 2027 and another $1.4 trillion in 2028. Although the semiconductor industry has benefited from strong demand, with the S&P Global Semiconductor Index rising approximately 95% through September, Moon Capital questioned whether the enormous infrastructure investments would generate adequate returns. The firm has avoided direct AI investments because it remains uncertain which companies will ultimately capture the economic benefits. The firm remains focused on businesses whose economics it can assess with confidence and whose shares trade at meaningful discounts to estimated intrinsic value. In addition, please check the Fund's top five holdings to know its best picks in 2026.

In its third-quarter 2026 investor letter, Moon Capital Management highlighted stocks like Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META). Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) stock closed at approximately $641.37 per share, with a market capitalization of about $1.64 trillion.

"The true economic costs of these expenditures aren't evident in the companies' earnings data. Chris Arnold

APLD

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Meta's Lease Could Back Up to $4.6 Billion in Louisiana Bonds for Applied Digital's AI Campus ©@panumas nikhomkhai from Pexels via Canva, @Karola G from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

A Louisiana public authority's Nov. 9 meeting packet includes a proposed agreement for up to $4.6 billion of revenue bonds to fund Applied Digital's Delta Forge 1 campus, to be repaid from its Meta lease.

Borrowing against Meta's lease could cost Applied Digital far less than the neocloud debt market, where Steve Eisman says a 15% cost of debt makes AI data centers prohibitively expensive.

Applied Digital's total debt rose to $5.1 billion in fiscal 2026, and its diluted share count has nearly quintupled since fiscal 2022, so a cheaper way to pay for construction matters.

The bonds are only proposed. There's no rate, no maturity and no final approval yet, so the terms are what to watch.

Applied Digital (APLD:NASDAQ) may have found a way to pay for its Louisiana AI campus on the strength of its tenant, Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ). A Louisiana public authority's latest meeting packet proposes up to $4.6 billion of bonds for the project, to be repaid from Meta's rent.

For a company that has paid for its growth with debt and new stock, that's a big deal.

TIKR tracks 16 analysts on Applied Digital. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Applied Digital, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Applied Digital's Analyst Ratings

What's in the Louisiana packet

A poster on Reddit's r/stocks flagged a 131-page packet for the Nov. 9 meeting of the England Economic and Industrial Development District. It includes a proposed agreement for:

Up to $4.6 billion of revenue bonds, which the district would sell to institutional investors to pay for building Delta Forge 1, a 300 MW campus in Boyce, La.

Payments on those bonds from Applied Digital's project subsidiary, with Louisiana taxpayers responsible for none of it.

A separate property-tax arrangement, with about $575 million of negotiated payments through 2052.

Meta is the campus's tenant, on a 15-year lease the poster puts at about $7.5 billion. Spread evenly, that's about $500 million a year, close to the $611 million of revenue Applied Digital booked in all of fiscal 2026 (the year ended May 2026). And analysts expect leases like this one to send its revenue sharply higher:

Applied Digital (APLD): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ millions, fiscal 2022-2029 (years to May) (TIKR)

I wouldn't expect a financing deal to move these estimates. The bigger question for shareholders is what that revenue costs to build.

Meta's lease is the real collateral

The cost of money matters a lot in AI right now. Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, pointed on the Nov. 6 episode of The Real Eisman Playbook to CoreWeave's debt being repriced from a yield of 9% to 15%, and said: "At a cost of debt of 15%, building AI data centers becomes prohibitively expensive." CoreWeave's bonds have since climbed to yields over 17%.

The results, which the company disclosed after the close on November 9, show a profit built mostly on non-cash investment gains. Underneath that headline, Trump Media's Truth API data licensing product is starting to generate recurring subscription revenue, and its core operating loss decreased.

Bitcoin Gains Power Trump Media's Q3 Profit

For Q3 2026, Trump Media posted net income of $409.75 million, compared with a net loss of $54.85 million a year earlier. That swing came from $496.1 million in non-cash realized and unrealized gains on digital assets and equity securities, partly offset by a derivatives loss and interest expense. Management tied the digital asset gain largely to the rise in Bitcoin during the quarter, meaning the profit reflects investment gains on the company's treasury. Stripping out those gains, Trump Media's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) loss decreased to $12.34 million from $29.06 million.

title: Billionaire David Rubenstein Passed On Facebook’s $30K Startup Pitch, Sold Amazon Before Billions In Gains. 'I Didn’t Take It Seriously'
detail:
Billionaire David Rubenstein Passed On Facebook’s $30K Startup Pitch, Sold Amazon Before Billions In Gains. 'I Didn’t Take It Seriously'
Image via Shutterstock

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

A billionaire investor's biggest regrets go back to the early days of the internet.

Carlyle Group (NASDAQ:CG) co-founder David Rubenstein passed on a chance to invest in Facebook. At the time, founder Mark Zuckerberg was trying to raise $30,000 to launch the site.

"I didn't take it seriously," he told Business Insider in September.

Rubenstein and his partners also sold their stake in Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN). He said the shares would have been worth billions if they'd held on.

Saverin Kept A Piece Of Facebook

Rubenstein said on the "Earn Your Leisure" podcast last month that he heard about Facebook from Evan Rachlin, one of Zuckerberg's Harvard classmates. 

Rachlin, who later became Rubenstein's son-in-law, told him the site would help students at Harvard find dates. Rubenstein had seen dating services come and go and didn't think Facebook would last. 

Another Harvard student, Eduardo Saverin, helped fund the launch. He left the company in 2005 and later settled a dispute over his stake. Saverin still owned shares when Facebook went public in 2012. 

Saverin co-founded venture capital firm B Capital in 2015. He's now based in Singapore, where he backs startups as the firm's co-CEO. Forbes says most of his wealth still comes from his shares in Facebook parent company Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META).

A Book Catalog Led To A 1% Stake

In Amazon's early days, Jeff Bezos offered book distributor Baker & Taylor a stake in the company for access to its catalog of books in print. Carlyle held a majority stake in the distributor, which has since shut down. 

Jeff Bezos offered Baker & Taylor a stake in Amazon for access to its catalog of books in print. Baker & Taylor turned down the shares and agreed to let Bezos use the catalog for five years at $100,000 a year, Rubenstein said on "Earn Your Leisure." 

When Rubenstein heard about the deal, he flew to Seattle to see if the original offer was still on the table. Bezos told him that two years had passed since the original offer and that he no longer needed Carlyle's help as much. He ended up with about 1% of Amazon.

title: BitGo adds APT stake to its growing Aptos relationship
detail:
BitGo adds APT stake to its growing Aptos relationship
Neo
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 10:57 AM MST 3 min read
APT21794-USD
META
Trade Aptos on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Crypto custody companies usually play the role of the neutral middleman. 

They hold digital assets for banks, funds and exchanges, and they rarely bet their own money on the networks they support. 

BitGo, one of the largest of them, is now putting its own balance sheet behind Aptos.

BitGo said that it has taken a "strategic position" in APT, the native token of the Aptos blockchain. 

Aptos is a layer-1 network, a base blockchain that apps are built on, originally incubated at Meta. APT is used to pay transaction fees and to help secure the network.

The company didn't disclose the size of the position, what it paid, or when it bought the tokens.

Related: $13 trillion brokerage giant offers cheapest ways to trade crypto

Building on years of Aptos support

BitGo is a New York Stock Exchange-listed company that stores digital assets for institutions. 

Its businesses include BitGo Bank & Trust, which the company describes as the first federally chartered digital asset trust bank owned by a publicly traded company.

The firm already offers Aptos services to its institutional clients. Eligible clients can store APT with BitGo and stake it, meaning they lock up tokens to help run the network in exchange for rewards. 

BitGo also holds assets created under the Aptos Digital Asset Standard, a framework for things like tokenized loans and real-world assets.

Abel Seow, BitGo's managing director and head of APAC sales, said the move continues that work. 

"Our work with Aptos already spans custody, staking, and connectivity to onchain markets," he said.

More on Aptos on TheStreet Roundtable:

A direct line to Decibel

That last part refers to Decibel, a trading platform built on Aptos and incubated by Aptos Labs, the network's core developer. 

Institutions that use BitGo's self-custody wallets can connect to Decibel through the same approval steps they already use for other transactions.

For Aptos, a custodian holding its token says something about confidence in the network's direction. 

Solomon Tesfaye, chief business officer at Aptos Labs, said BitGo's stake "underscores its commitment to Aptos."

Michael Ching, head of treasury and operations at the Aptos Foundation, the nonprofit that supports the network's growth, described it in terms of what institutions look for. 

"Institutional adoption tends to follow solid infrastructure," he said.
